content.text:
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
The project will deliver 23% in cost savings or $8 million, significantly improving the economics and also providing some additional benefits, such as reducing our surface footprint and lowering the emissions from fewer wellbores. We expect the well performance from the horseshoe wells will match that of our regular 10,000-foot laterals. Once this technology becomes more de-risked, we can further increase the average lateral length in our inventory by converting short laterals into long laterals and further enhancing our efficiencies. I'll now hand the call back over to Jay to summarize our outlook.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Okay, Dan. Thank you, Roland. Thank you. You know, Dan, you're talking about the horseshoe wells. I'm thinking about the majority owner of the stock is, owns the Dallas Cowboys. Cowboys and horseshoes go together. Thank you for that report. Let's go to page 15. I direct you to Slide 15, where we summarize our outlook for 2024. As we stated in the last quarter, we really have taken a number of steps in response to the significantly low natural gas prices this year. During Q1, we announced we'd release two of our operated drilling rigs. We reduced our rig count to five rigs. We also released one of our frac spreads, reducing our frac spreads to two spreads. We no longer now have any long-term commitments for our pressure pumping services.
With those steps and our 2024 CapEx is expected to be down 34% to 41% from the 2023 level. We suspended our quarterly dividend. That saved about $140 million a year in dividend payments. In late March, our majority stakeholder, Jerry Jones, invested an additional $105 million into the company through an equity placement that the company had. Starting in late February, you know, we did add significantly to our hedge position starting in Q4 2024 and extending that through the year-end 2026. We're targeting a hedge level of 50% of our expected production level through those years.
In early April, we further enhanced our liquidity position with a $400 million senior notes offering, and we continued to maintain a very strong financial liquidity, which totaled just under $1.2 billion at the end of Q2. Our industry-leading lowest cost structure is an asset in the current low natural gas price environment, as our cost structure is substantially lower than the other public natural gas producers. We remain very, very focused on improving upon our Western Haynesville play and continuing to add to our extensive acreage position in this exciting play. Our Western Haynesville acreage position totals over 450,000 net acres to date.
We believe that we're building a great asset in the Western Haynesville that will be well-positioned to benefit from the substantial growth and demand for natural gas in our region that is on the horizon, driven by the growth in LNG exports that began to show up in H2 of next year. I'll now turn it over to Ron to provide specifics for the rest of the year. Ron?
Ron Mills
VP of Finance and Investor Relations, Comstock Resources
Thanks, Jay. On Slide 16, we provide some financial guidance for Q3 and the remainder of 2024. For Q3, we expect our D&C CapEx to range between $135 and $185 million, and our full year D&C guidance range on CapEx remains $750 to$ 850 million. The midstream capital outlook remains unchanged, and the leasing capital for Q3 and Q4 remains in the $2 to $5 million range. The full year moved up $5 to $10 million just due to actual Q2 leasing costs. LOE and GTC costs both for Q3 and Q4, and full year remain unchanged from prior levels.
On the production and ad valorem, the guidance range remains the same, which includes the impact of a lower severance tax rate in Louisiana basically being offset by a higher ad valorem rate. The DD&A rate, as mentioned by Roland earlier, is expected to be higher through the remainder of the year, due to the current low prices. Looking ahead, though, we would anticipate that to return to our more normal level, in the kind of price environment that we see in 2025. No other changes to our G&A or interest outlook that we provided in prior quarters, and we continue to anticipate deferring virtually 100% of our deferred taxes. With that, I'll turn the call over to the operator for Q&A.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. To remove yourself from the queue, you may press star one one again. We ask that you please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up to allow everyone the opportunity to participate. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from the line of Carlos Escalante of Wolfe Research.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Hey, good morning, gentlemen. Thank you for taking my question.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Good morning.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Good morning. If I use the Q2 completed wells as a proxy for your drilling pace on wells under 5,000 feet, I'm getting a number that is roughly less than 10% per quarter. Bearing in mind your horseshoe concept update, how do you all see the allocation towards a potentially successful program going into the future quarters and future years? Thank you.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
You know, this is Dan. I'll kind of address just the short laterals. We did have one short lateral that we reported here. We had basically really already kind of had drilled that well when we had our last call. You know, I think with the success of the horseshoe concept, I think really the majority of all the wells, short wells that we have in our inventory will convert to long laterals. But there will be a few where we've just got maybe one short lateral left, and that's all that's left to be drilled, you know, and it's bounded by other wells where, you know, if you did decide to drill, that's you have to drill a short lateral.
We won't be able to convert all of them to 10K horseshoe wells, but I think you know, a good chunk of the inventory we'll be able to convert to 10Ks.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Wonderful. I might follow up real quick on that same topic. I think that the fact that it's less than 10% that you're drilling at that specific land sort of emphasizes why market may be able or may be reticent to recognize that inventory when you say 25 to 30 years of inventory. On that same topic, Dan, what's the end goal here? Is it more of a recognition of what the risk may be on the concept? Or is this the first one for many to come?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
I think this is the first of many to come. Just like with anything that's new, you know, I think the public wants to see more of them drilled. They wanna see it become routine. They wanna see it de-risked. I think they, you know, they're probably a little bit further into that process in the other basins, I think really mainly the Permian and I think a few in the Eagle Ford or the horseshoe wells. There was one drilled earlier this year and it was problem free. You know, like I said, we're almost at TD on the one that we're drilling, and it's been problem free to date. You know, we feel really good about it.
I think we'll, we feel really good about, you know, significantly reducing the short laterals in our inventory. We'll have more 10Ks. Our average lateral length will be up. Our efficiencies will be way up. We just need to do more, you know, where it becomes routine and, you know, to take some of the risk out.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, like Dan said, if you save $8 million when you drill these wells, a couple of them, that does add to our inventory because some of these wells we've pushed back to the latter part of our drilling inventory. Now if you have these cost savings, you can bring them forward if you need to drill them.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Right. You know, some of these we've drilled because we've, you know, we've had them for a while and some of the production gets low, so we just, to protect our leasehold, you know, is why we'll put some of these on our drilling schedule.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Wonderful. Thank you, gentlemen.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Jake Roberts of TPH&Co.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Morning.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Morning.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Wanted to dig in a bit more on the Baker wells and some of the issues that you highlighted. Can you speak to any correlation between what occurred and the IP rates? Is there any impact to the EUR we might expect? Does this mean that region is something that might need to be avoided in the future?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, it's certainly out on the edge of, you know, our acreage footprint. That is, we do know from past drilling up in that area that the well bore's stability is a little bit more, you know, the rock itself just has a little bit more instability. Really we had. Normally that area up there typically drills, you know, the drilling cost is a little bit more expensive, maybe, you know, $1,650 to $1,700 a foot's kinda normal, whereas back over in Texas in the state line area, you know we're in that $1,450 to $1,500 a foot. We drilled five wells. Two of the wells were the ones that really gave us problems. We ended up had one well drilled to TD. We lost the lateral.
We tried to sidetrack it. We ended up having to sidetrack it twice to get it drilled, and we had basically another well that we had two sidetracks on. It wasn't a very pleasant experience, but it's definitely an outlier. If you look at just kind of where all our acreage is, it's out on the edge. You know, we knew that area was kind of tough to drill, so just, it's just a one-time event. It was you know, we drilled it because the acreage was expiring. We had to drill it or lose it. We did decide to do full development and drill five wells all the way across the section. You know, that's just a one-time event.
I think if you do pull that out, we're back around that $1,500 a foot total D&C cost for this quarter, which is where we'll be at for Q3 and Q4.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Okay, great. I appreciate that. My second question. The two-well pad sounds like the drilling is wrapped up. We appreciate the update on the days to drill, but can you give us a sense of where cost per foot is sitting on the drilling side of things, now that you're done?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. Actually we see costs, you know, going down a little bit. We actually started seeing a big movement in pipe prices just here the last couple of months. We're working through inventory that we already have, but I think by the time we get to wells that turn to sales in Q1 that we're completing right at the end of Q4, we're seeing some significant savings on pipe cost. We'll definitely should see our D&C costs, you know, basically come down Q3 and really further into Q4 and Q1.
Bertrand Donnes
Financial Analyst, Truist Securities
Great. Appreciate the time, guys.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Charles Meade of Johnson Rice.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice & Company
Good morning, Jay, Roland, Dan, and Ron.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Hey, Charles.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Hi, Charles.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice & Company
I wanted to ask a question. Dan, I think you partially answered this in your prepared remarks, but I just wanna make sure I heard it right, maybe get an elaboration. When I was looking at your Q3 CapEx, it's both down versus Q2, but it's also a pretty wide range on the upper and lower bound, at least it seems that way to me. Dan, I think I heard you say in your prepared comments that you recently dropped one of your two frac crews. You're gonna let it. You're just gonna be running one crew for August and September. It sounds like you're gonna pick it up again. Did I hear that right?
Is that the driver of the CapEx decline in Q3?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yes.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice & Company
What other pieces are there that maybe contribute to a wide range?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, I think it's not totally that, but that's the kind of significant driver. You know, that's just kind of a reflection of dropping the rigs earlier in the year. I mean, obviously, we've got less wells to complete. We went from three to two, I think, basically right at the first of the year. We've been running two all year. We just gapped this one frac crew probably a couple of weeks ago. We're slated to pick it up around, like, the first week of October. We also, you know, just like I mentioned earlier, we see the cost coming down. The pipe prices are coming down significantly finally. That's kinda one of the last pieces where we've seen the prices come down.
You know, we've already seen the rig costs come down a little bit, the frac costs come down a little bit earlier this year. Just overall, the cost, you know, cost of services coming down, coupled with that one frac crew being gone for, you know, two out of the three months for Q3 is the driver on CapEx.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice & Company
Got it. That is helpful detail. The question about the drilling times in the Western Haynesville. You guys highlighted the 54 days. Can you put that in some bigger context of, you know, where your early wells fell on how many days it took to drill, and also what you think is a reasonable goal for days to drill in the next 12 or 18 months?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, I think so we've made great progress on our drilling days to TD in the Western Haynesville. Now, the wells have been different lengths, you know, so that kinda comes into place on the number of days, especially in the Western Haynesville with the higher temperatures. But we, you know, we generally were around, like, that 85-day mark when we started, and we've shaved it down to these last couple of wells on these two-well pads were 54 and 56 days. So, you know, that's pretty significant, and I think there's still some running room there. We're still, you know, got some efficiencies we look to gain, you know, drilling in the laterals. So I think we can move that number down a little bit but
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You might add that those with the low number of days, those were long laterals, correct?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. Those were both, I think one of them was a 10,000-foot lateral, one was just under an 11,000-foot lateral. So.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice & Company
Got it.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
those were both in the Haynesville with the higher temperatures. I mean, that's kind of the, you know, everything we've drilled to date, it's basically what I'd say are the toughest wells that we've drilled, you know, basically TDs, lateral lengths, temperatures. Yeah, we've made a big improvement there. You know, like I said, we still are working on a few things to work those numbers down a little bit lower.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, Charles, from the first well to the sixteenth well, you know, you go from 85 days to 54 days. That's 31 days you save. That's a whole month's drilling. You know, even if you use 26, 27, that means that the wells that we're drilling now, I mean, we've saved half the time. If it's 54 days and we've already shaved off 26, 7 days. These wells, you'll probably end up drilling another well per year because of our drilling efficiencies with the same number of rigs, it could equate to that. That is huge savings, and, you know, your questions are on cost savings. At 31 days of drilling with these deeper, hotter wells, that saves a lot of money.
Charles Meade
Research Analyst, Johnson Rice & Company
Got it. Thank you. That's helpful context, Jay and Dan.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
You bet. Thanks, Charles.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Bertrand Donnes of Truist.
Bertrand Donnes
Financial Analyst, Truist Securities
Hey, good morning, guys. Just staying on the Horseshoe wells. The example you give looks very promising on the cost side. I know it's early, but are there any expectations on the productivity of these wells? Do you get the full amount that you would have gotten from the two shorter, you know, shorter laterals, or do you kinda lose, like, 5% of the recoveries? And how does the shape of that well look like? Is it a lower, you know, pro forma IP than maybe the two combined wells, but a lower decline, or any thoughts there?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's a really good question. You know, we definitely expect the performance to be the same as the 10K well. You know, the only really mild difference between a horseshoe well and a 10,000-foot, you know, across two sections of straight lateral is on the straight lateral, you do get complete across the section line, you know, that 660-foot. You know, the state you can't perforate within 330-foot of the lease line. You know, you basically got two 4,600-foot sections, 9,200-foot. We're on a 10K, so on a straight 10K, you get to perforate a little bit more, you know, as far as the amount that's completed across the 10K.
On a per unit basis, we expect the performance to be totally the same.
Bertrand Donnes
Financial Analyst, Truist Securities
That's great color. Thanks. Shifting gears on the private side of the Haynesville, you know, we can see some of the data on our side. It looks like there's been some drops on the rig side throughout the year, but over the last four months or so, it's been kind of stable. I'm just wondering if you have a temperature check maybe on the private operators in your discussions with them. You know, do you get the impression that they've already settled into a steady program, or are they also looking at the strip right now and actively debating maybe dropping some activity?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, we really don't have a lot of insight other than kind of knowing how we coordinate our schedules with the other operators. I think, yeah, the private operators, you know, cut rigs back very dramatically, and they're kinda kept that same rate. You know, we haven't seen any increase in activity that's on the horizon. I think they're waiting to really see, you know, when gas prices, you know, kind of justify that. The higher rig count has been on the public side, you know, mainly with Southwestern.
Bertrand Donnes
Financial Analyst, Truist Securities
Yeah.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
You know, other than that, everybody else but them has dropped a lot of rigs.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. I agree with Roland. I think you'll basically kind of stay status quo until everybody sees these gas prices move up.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, if you look at the core, is that 9,000 square miles, what they call the core. When you drill a well there, either Bossier or Haynesville, you've got a 40% decline in the first year. You need to be real careful about drilling at a $1.90 gas price. Whereas in, like in the Western Haynesville, we hadn't seen that type of decline. That would be another reason, whether you're private or public, that you don't aggressively drill these wells.
Bertrand Donnes
Financial Analyst, Truist Securities
That's a great point. Thanks, guys.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Kevin MacCurdy of Pickering Energy Partners.
Kevin MacCurdy
Director of Research, Pickering Energy Partners
Hey, good morning, guys. I wanted to ask about activity toggles. Now that the debt covenant is of less concern, just given the state of gas prices, is there any situation which would result in the frac holiday extending into Q4? Or are there any other changes you would consider this year to activity levels?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
I think the frac holiday is. I think we pretty much got it set. I don't really see it extending further into Q4, you know, just based on what we know today and where we see prices going. I mean, really kind of a short answer there, but I think our schedule, we kinda look at it pretty set.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
We look at it all the time, so we can obviously pull those levers if we see that. You still see, you know, gas prices improving as you get to the very end of the year. You know, so I think unless kind of 2025 changes.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Dramatically, I think that's kind of what would drive our activity level in Q4.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Right. We're, you know, we're not contractually obligated, obviously, with the frac crews. I mean, we could definitely, you know, shift things. You know, the outlook really changed. I mean, obviously, we can change with it.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, fortunately, in the Q4, we do hit our swap position where we're hedged 50% at that $3.50. Now that's something that if prices do continue to deteriorate, we will at least end up in that quarter. You know, we have, I think we've adequately hedged for 2025, 2026 so far, with 35% of our production hedged at the $3.50+ range. As we said in the opening, you know, our goal is to hedge at least 50% of all of the 2025, 2026 production. We are getting out of the 20+% hedge environment into the 50% environment.
Kevin MacCurdy
Director of Research, Pickering Energy Partners
Thanks for that. That's helpful. Just wanted to ask, did any of the Q2 weather impacts spill into Q3, or did you guys see any impacts from the hurricane?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
We did have impacts from the hurricane. Basically it, Hurricane Beryl. When it moved up into, we didn't have any impacts in our Western Haynesville area, but when it moved up into our core area, there were just, it really, you know, spawned a ton of tornadoes. Really the thing that hurts us is not necessarily our operations, but all the treating, you know, third-party treating facilities that we flow to, basically, you know, they go down and lost power. It really does, you know, it really hurts our production. We're just kinda at their mercy. We did have that for approximately a week to 10 days in July.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
That impact is incorporated in the Q3 guidance.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, correct.
Kevin MacCurdy
Director of Research, Pickering Energy Partners
Appreciate it. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Leo Mariani of Roth.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Yeah, guys. Wanted to just dig in a little bit more into kind of expectations heading into the Q4. I think you guys have previously talked about Q4 production being down around 10%, you know, year-over-year. I know a couple of wells kind of slipped, you know, into January potentially. I wanted to see if that's still, you know, roughly valid. With respect to, you know, Q4 CapEx, looks like that's getting ready to maybe move a little higher as the frac crew comes back. Just trying to get a sense, should Q4 CapEx look more like Q2 of 2024 CapEx?
Ron Mills
VP of Finance and Investor Relations, Comstock Resources
Good questions. There's no change on that in terms of Q4 2024 versus Q4 2023. You know, it looks like it can be down about 10%. You know, as we've talked about, that's a function of the timing of dropping those two rigs in February and March, and kind of that 6- to 9-month lag between dropping activity and seeing it show up in production. You're absolutely right. The CapEx level in Q4 will return more to the level that you mentioned. A lot of that is a function of what we've discussed earlier with the frac holiday all occurring in Q3. That's why Q3 and Q4 are so different in terms of CapEx levels.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well in the Western Haynesville, yeah. Really no wells coming on in H2 for the most part. Then a lot of, you know, a lot of production coming on in the Western Haynesville right around the end of the year.
You know, maybe a few wells are online right before that and a lot in early January. We actually like the way that lines up with, you know, the gas market and all that, so.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, Leo, that's the Hogue-Duple, the two-well pad analysis. Those are our wells we drilled on the pads, the two per pad, and then the horseshoe and the Miles. That's the wells, you know, really the last week of December maybe, or the first week of January 2025. That's when we've modeled it to come in.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Okay. No, that's very helpful color.
I know obviously, you know, 2025, you know, a little early here for that today. Just trying to get a sense, I mean, looking at strip prices for next year, kind of $3.25 to $3.30 currently. As you look out, is that the right level that you think for Comstock to kind of get back to where it was and add a couple rigs to kind of get back to the seven rigs? Is that kind of how you're thinking about it here today, is to kind of bring those rigs back, you know, kind of early next year?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that price level is real. Yeah. Obviously, it is definitely works well for Comstock. You know, it's still early. Like I said, we don't really set our activity for next year until we get more into the Q4 and then November, even December, and make those decisions. I mean, yeah, we do like the way that, you know, what the futures market has out there. We'll just see if that materializes. Then having a stronger hedge position, you know, will also help support that program, you know, in 2025 than what we had, you know, coming into 2024.
Leo Mariani
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, ROTH MKM
Okay. Thanks, guys.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thanks, Leo.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Neil Mehta of Goldman Sachs.
Neil Mehta
Managing Director, Goldman Sachs
Yeah. Good morning, team. Thanks for taking the time. Two questions. The first was just your perspective on the A&D market. How do you think about both acquisitions or potential proceeds from divestitures as we make our way over the course of the next year? Are there opportunities to optimize on a smaller scale or even medium to larger sized bolt-ons?
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, I mean, we've had incoming opportunities all the time. We look at all of them. You know, some of them we react to and go forward in, like acquiring the acreage that we did the last quarter. Our real focus right now is to you know end the outspend and get our production going up, not going down. We need to take care of that. Our inbound calls that we have, they're mainly data centers that wanna do business with us. They're utilities, they're storage, they're more acreage, a little bit of acreage to clean up what we have at least, and Ron has budgeted for that.
As like we said in the very beginning, our goal is if the M&A market is about inventory, our goal is that with the 450,000+ net acres in Western Haynesville, we should have incredible inventory adds, that goes with the 1,400 locations that we have in our core. That's really our goal. Our goal is like a Dan Harrison focus, and that's operations. You know, you test your geological group, and we've tested that group for four years. We've had successful wells, and with success, we've added new acreage. Each of the wells seems to be a little bit better. They're a little different, but they seem to be a little better.
You know, the question that was asked earlier, if you can drill these wells in 54 days, well, now if you drill two of those wells in 54 days, you almost add a third well compared to the 85 days that we used to drill these in. That's efficiencies in numbers, saves you a lot of money. Like, every two wells in the old day, now you get a third well for the same amount of money. That's the efficiencies that we see. If we continue to prove out the geology, continue to test the seismic that we have in the area. The wells continue to perform like they have and clean up like they have.
I think our goal is just to prove that we created great wealth when the market comes to us with this great gas demand for power generation, and LNG, and industrial demand. That's our focus. We've spent a lot of money putting together this world-class footprint in the Western Haynesville, and now we just wanna de-risk it well by well. We're not on a big M&A binge at all.
Neil Mehta
Managing Director, Goldman Sachs
Yeah, that's great perspective. The follow-up is just, you know, one question we get asked a lot is sort of the breakevens of the Western Haynesville. When you think of your cost of supply to earn a cost to capital return fully burdened for G&A and interest and all the ancillary, what is that breakeven in your mind for Henry Hub equivalent?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, yeah, of course, it's evolving in the Western Haynesville as we're continuing to work down the drilling and completion cost. Kinda where we see the cost being, you know, with the efficient program that we'll have next year with four rigs and kinda, you know, with the pad drilling that starts to get it more on par with our traditional Haynesville. We actually, the two areas are gonna be very similar as far as internal rate of return and cost per reserves found. I mean, the difference is we have a lot more money in a Western Haynesville well, but we have a lot more reserves. I mean, the reserves are double. It's a different type of play.
The declines are different. There's, you know, we're still trying to figure out how to produce the Western Haynesville wells. There's a difference there that you get probably a little bit more production out of a traditional Haynesville well in the first, you know, six months. You know, the second six months, you'll get a lot more production out of a Western Haynesville well, 'cause the way we're producing them with a much tighter choke. In the end, they're very comparable and, you know, as far as returns, especially where we see the cost getting to now that we're kind of getting into a more development stage. We're very pleased with that.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, I think to add on to that, if you look at this inventory depletion, which will happen, you know, you run out of tier ones, you go to tier twos. The bang for the buck is not quite there in tier two or three because you run out of tier ones. If our Western Haynesville is compared to tier one, and we have all this acreage, and we de-risk it, our inventory is gonna be materially stronger than you'd have if you did a big M&A. M&A is just acquiring more in the same area.
Neil Mehta
Managing Director, Goldman Sachs
Thanks, team.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Phillips Johnston of Capital One Securities.
Phillips Johnston
Senior E&P Analyst, Capital One Securities
Hey, thanks for taking the question. It's really a follow-up to Leo's question. The 2025 plan is obviously very much TBD. You know, if you do stay at five rigs for the balance of the year, and you bring that frac crew back in Q4, you know, as you look out into the first few months of next year, just from a momentum perspective, would you expect your volumes to be directionally flat, up, or down versus Q4 levels?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
They'll definitely be up with those Western Haynesville wells coming on.
Phillips Johnston
Senior E&P Analyst, Capital One Securities
Yeah.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Phillips Johnston
Senior E&P Analyst, Capital One Securities
Okay. That's all. Thanks, Roland.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Thank you, Phillips.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Noel Parks of Tuohy Brothers Investment Research.
Noel Parks
Managing Director of Energy Research, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Hey, it's Noel. Good to talk to you. Just had a couple I wanted to run by you. In terms of the Western Haynesville with the greater depth and the heat and pressure and so forth, I was wondering if you could talk a bit about where things stand with the instruments and tools that I understand have had some adaptation to be able to work at those levels. Just where are you? Is any of that you're doing proprietary? Anything new that you're gonna be implementing in the next slate of wells?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
No, this is Dan. You know, we basically use the same tools in the Western Haynesville that we use in the core. You know, we basically, you know, how we apply them, you know, is a little bit differently. You know, as far as our MWD tools, our motors, you know, essentially the same providers, you know, for the Western Haynesville that we have, you know, that we have in the core. Now, there's some, you know, there's some of our providers up in the core that, you know, can't, you know, doesn't have the full breadth of tools to be able to work in the Western Haynesville. You know, the same guys we have working down there work in the core also. Same tools.
Noel Parks
Managing Director of Energy Research, Tuohy Brothers Investment Research
Got it. You just mentioned, or Roland just mentioned, how you produce the Western Haynesville wells and the effect that might have on declines and so forth. I don't know. Just what are your thoughts, where are you going so far about, you know, choking and how that might influence, you know, production rates, shape of the curve, et cetera?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, we definitely started off in the Western Haynesville being much more conservative with how we were producing the wells compared to how we produce them in the core. Obviously, we've got years and years and years of history in the core, and we know, you know, how we can produce them and how hard we can pull them. In the Western Haynesville, we're just on the tip of that learning curve. So we started out very conservative, you know, very low drawdowns. You know, we've kind of just, we're slowly kind of starting to maybe pulling them just a little bit harder and get a little bit better production rates, which they can definitely do it.
We just wanna watch the drawdowns and make sure, you know, we don't get ahead of ourselves as far as trying to pull them too hard. Everything looks really good. We're just kinda taking our time, you know, in that process.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
We produce through tubing, you meant, over that.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah. We do. Everything that we complete up in the core, you know, we flow up the casing for quite a long time. We don't come back and tube up those wells for, you know, in some cases, maybe a couple of years, you know, later. In the Western Haynesville, just because of the very high initial, you know, flowing pressures from what the well head with the casing, you know, the burst pressure rating is on our casing strings, we tube those up while we're completing the well. The day that they turn to sales, all those wells are flowing up tubing. It's a little bit different production profile. You get a lot more pressure drop, you know, down hole before you reach the surface.
You know, the pressures obviously would be a lot higher if we were flowing up casing, the surface pressures would. But that's probably the biggest difference, you know, as far as, you know, downhole. All the Western Haynesville wells are tubed up. All the core wells flow up casing.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, you're asking about the drilling. If you look at our efficiencies, and Dan's right, I mean, some of the tools and the casing, we do use that in the core, but it's how you use it. What type of intermediate do you set? Do you tube the wells up? What type of completions do you have? What kind of drill pipe do you have? I mean, there's a lot of ingredients in the kitchen, and not everybody produces the same final product. So it can be very difficult if you're drilling your first 19,000-foot vertical and 10,000-foot lateral well to come in there and have the success that we've had when you've got a really good operations group, and it took them 85 days the first time. Well, now you're at 54 days.
A lot of that skill set, you have to spend a lot of money to perfect it. When you can perfect it, then you can lower those costs, and you create real wealth. You have to have the footprint to do that in. We captured a footprint at very low cost with most of it being held by production. That's the difference in this play.
Carlos Escalante
VP and Senior Associate, Wolfe Research
Great. Thanks a lot.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Paul Diamond of Citi.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Hi, good morning. Thanks for taking my call. Just a quick one. Wanted to drill down on the opportunity set across these, the theoretical horseshoe wells. In your inventory, you got about, call it 16-odd% of, you know, below 5,000 foot. I'm just trying to understand how much of those, you know, given current expectations, you think you might be able to convert and where that would place them kind of in the, in the larger, production cadence or drilling cadence?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's a really good question. You're right, we do have about 15% or 16% of our total inventory is, you know, the short laterals. We're actually currently working through that process right now of how many of those we think we can convert over to long laterals. I think the majority of them that we can, I don't really have a real, you know, fixed number I can probably give you today. I'd say the majority of them we're looking at moving over. You know, like I said, the only reason that we could not would just be because, I mean, obviously, you have to have two, you know, you have to have two of the 5,000 laterals kinda side by side, right, to have the horseshoe opportunity.
Some of our short sticks in our inventory, you know, you just got one stick, basically. Obviously, that wouldn't be a horseshoe candidate. You know, other than that, I think every, you know, if you got two of them side by side, every one of those is a horseshoe candidate. We're working through that process right now, seeing which one of those we can, you know, convert. They'll go in our long lateral bucket, which right now, you know, that's about 26% of our inventory. We'll significantly boost that up above, you know, 25-26% and, you know, that percentage in the short laterals will get a lot lower, which will be great.
I mean, that opens up a lot more wells that has really good economics that we can basically, you know, decide to put on our drill schedule. Or should we, you know, for some reason, for a leasehold reason or whatever, we kinda need to drill it, you know, it'll still fit in with the, you know, what we normally would be drilling with good economics.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. That actually kinda pertains to my follow-up. Assuming or under current assumptions you guys are working with, how would a horseshoe, you know, two 5,000-foot compare economically to an existing 10,000-foot?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yes, substantial. I don't have numbers in front of me, but yes, substantial, you know, rate of return, substantial improvement. I mean, you're gonna save $8 million, $4 million per basically off those 5K laterals. You know, it just drives all the key parameters significantly higher. Like I said, the cost. The cost to drill a straight 10K, to drill a horseshoe well is essentially the same. You know, I said a 1% to 2% premium, but I mean, that's within the plus or minus of any well we drill on kind of where our costs are gonna end up. You know, we look at the economics for a horseshoe well to be essentially the same as all of our other 10K laterals.
Paul Diamond
Equity Research Analyst, Citi
Understood. Thanks, Roland.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Gregg Brody of Bank of America.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
Hey, good day. Good afternoon, guys. Thanks for all the update. As the credit guy, I've started to see these horseshoe wells pop up a few places, and I realize there's some data. There's been a number of them in other basins. I'm just curious, is there something that we should think about that is tricky about these, or it really is just drilling a lateral in a U-shape that seems like physics suggests we can do that now?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Right. You know, sometimes, the old saying, necessity is the mother of invention. I mean, you know, you drill a 90-degree turn to drill these laterals already, right? You know, you do the 90-degree turn, you're drilling the lateral. It's the same tools, it's the same motors that we run. You just make another turn, and you just stay with it until it goes all the way around 180 degrees. Now, I think, you know, until you kinda have to do it, you know, or, you know, you're looking at your inventory, talking about improvement. You know, a lot of people probably just kinda don't push to go there. Really the...
I mean, look, there is a little bit more risk to drilling a horseshoe well and you know, you gotta get casing around the curve. You have to get you know, when you're completing and pumping your perforating guns down and plugs you know, for all your frack stages you know, all those have to get pumped around the curve. I mean, but really, that's. I think the risk of that's pretty small. The industry kinda already has shown it in the Permian and I think the Eagle Ford for these other areas. You know, I think you just gotta prove it out, and you just basically gotta show people the results. I think you know, after you do more of them, it becomes a little bit more routine, and the risk is you know, greatly diminished.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Well, for example, on our first well, I mean, we're pretty close to TD in that well. Last night, I know we were-
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
We're probably within 500 foot of TD.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
We have had zero problems drilling the well.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, that's my point. First well, no problems. We're within 500 feet to TD in it.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
You were being asked earlier about how much potential of your locations could be converted. Should we think that it's just the ones that are in the up to 5,000 feet, or should we think also about the 5,000 to 8,500 feet that could be converted? Just trying to get.
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, it really.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
Just trying to get a sense of how much of that. You didn't quantify it. I know it's early days, but
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Yeah.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
I'm curious if you have a range that you would think about there?
Dan Harrison
COO, Comstock Resources
Well, that's a really good question, and we've already kinda had some internal discussions about that. You know, can you take a 7,500-foot lateral and turn it into a 15K horseshoe? Now, we're not ready to kinda jump out there and do that yet. Look, the industry gets better with time. They get faster, they get longer, tools get better. If you have the demand for tools and the demand for certain services, in time, they show up, and they get developed, and they get refined. I think in time, I think, yes. I think that the industry will maybe go there. I mean, look, a 7,500-foot lateral has a lot better economics than a 5K, so the rush to start doing 15K horseshoes is not really gonna be there right now.
I do see, you know, and it's what your acreage, it's how it's laid out and what, you know, your options are. You know, I mean, you if you got two sections or three sections, you know, like we'll typically just drill a 15K straight lateral. We're not gonna do a bunch of 7,500-foot horseshoe 15K laterals. You know what I mean? That's. It's a very good question, and I think yes. I think in time in the future, I think there'll probably be some people that will probably try to push the horseshoe lengths a little bit further. The one, you know, they do have a little bit more torque and drag.
I mean, obviously, when you're pushing and pulling pipe around a 180-degree bend, it adds more drag, you know, push, you know, tripping in and out of the hole. You know, a 10,000-foot horseshoe well is kinda maybe more like the equivalent of a 15,000-foot straight lateral when you look at the drag going in and out of the hole, if that makes sense.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
That does. Just to come back to my credit roots, just a few follow-ups that you might get for some credit guys. I don't see you getting a... You're at 3.4 today. I think you're okay for next quarter to get into 3 to 5 or not going through the 3.5. Is that fair? If not, is it just a pretty easy amendment that you would get? Just as part of that, you know, I know the dividend was suspended this year. Just as you look out in the future, how do you think about that today?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, Greg. Of course, obviously, the gas prices are, you know, if we knew exactly what they were, we could answer the question exactly. That, you know, the gas prices and where they end up being will be a big driver in the EBITDA, which is the biggest part of that ratio. You know, it's also, kind of, remember, it's a kind of a full four-quarter calculation assessed in one quarter. Yeah, we stay pretty close to that level. We do think we can get a temporary waiver if we needed it, but we didn't need it, so, you know, we didn't go out and get it. So things kinda came in exactly as we thought they would.
We knew we were gonna get to that 3-4, luckily, we stayed there. We'll monitor it in Q3, you know, as hard as we monitored it in Q2.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Okay.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Then the dividend, obviously, I think we're, you know, we're not really talking about a dividend, you know, until we kinda get the leverage way down and, you know, looking off in the future. I think our first priority, you know, is to get back to generating good free cash flow, and then that will be used for some debt reduction to get the leverage ratio, you know, back to. We'd like to get back to levels that we were seeing, you know, back in 2022. You know, like we got to under, you know, closer to one times leverage.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
You know, we were really monitoring Q2, and again, we did stay fine. In Q3, we didn't expect gas to be $1.90 on Monday. You do look at that price and say, Well, okay, so you gotta really monitor Q3. In Q4, you know, we would expect a little price appreciation and the hedges come in and help. After that, I think we're gonna have some big production growth. So that's it. We're kinda going through that valley right now. It's a good question.
Gregg Brody
High Yield Research Analyst, Bank of America
I appreciate the time, guys, and the education.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Thank you, Greg.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Geoff Jay of Daniel Energy Partners.
Geoff Jay
Partner, Daniel Energy Partners
Hey, guys. Just a real quick one for me. Earlier, you said you would expect to see D&C costs go down to something like normal levels. I guess I've kinda forgotten what normal looks like given all the inflation we've seen over the last year or so. Where do you kinda think those will trend given the service cost inflation that's out there and the efficiencies you're achieving?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Well, we think our legacy Haynesville, you know, main product, you know, will trend back to that, you know, a little bit below $1,500. That's $1,500. $1,400 to $1,500 is kind of an area, you know. I think, you know, the way we report this is kinda when wells are completed and they. You know, it's not really a good indication of where things are now because some of the wells we completed this quarter were actually drilled last year. Maybe we'll come back and add some additional information here and show you, here's the real drilling costs being incurred each quarter, and here's the completion costs being incurred.
They'll be on different wells, but they'd be more indicative of where costs are versus the process here of scoring is costs that were incurred in, you know, different periods than the one you're hearing about, so. Also, if you have a certain group of wells, you know, that are different and they're more costly, that happen to be the ones turned to sales, they dominate the numbers. As is the case this quarter, you have these Lake Bistineau wells that have a lot of. It's a high-cost area, period, and plus you throw some drilling problems in, and those wells kinda really distorted, you know, what would've been just looked pretty comparable to the other quarter if they weren't in there.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
We got less wells to average it down.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Yeah, we'll probably try to maybe provide some supplemental. You know, that will allow you to see the current cost of the quarter, how they're trending, you know, versus seeing something that occurred maybe, you know, even last year.
Bertrand Donnes
Financial Analyst, Truist Securities
Excellent. Well, thank you for that.
Operator
Thank you. I would now like to turn the conference back to Jay Allison for closing remarks. Sir.
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
All right. Thank you again. We've gone over our hour, but as you know, the company, we've always had a vision. I think Greg asked about, you know, do you drill these horseshoe wells that are 7,500 foot to times two, 15,000 feet? The answer is, we have a vision, and we had a vision to step out 100 miles and see if we could rebirth a major gas play, which is now the Western Haynesville. We have a vision, and then we always monitor where gas supply is. If you look, we've been looking for the last probably six or seven weeks, and that gas storage level is about 38% above the five-year average. Well, week after week after week, that's come down. It's like 16% above the five-year average.
It's coming the right way, and we're coming into the three, four, five weeks of what we call the real meat of the summer. We do see that. We see LNG at over 13 Bs a day right now. It's back. Freeport is back. Then we look past September, October, and you see the startups of Corpus Christi Stage 3 in Plaquemines. We see a strong Q4 2024 run from the LNG fleet, and that goes into 2025. We're committed to sharing everything that we can share in all of our areas and to protect our balance sheet.
again, I wanna compliment the Joneses for, you know, writing the $100 million check for the acreage that we've been acquiring. I think that acreage is worth a fortune, and they were willing to backstop that and write the check. We're gonna be in good shape there. Thank you for your time. We appreciate it.
Operator
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Operator
Thank you for standing by, and welcome to the Comstock Resources First Quarter 2023 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentations, there'll be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question at that time, please press star one one on your telephone. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to your host, Mr. Jay Allison, Chairman and CEO. Please go ahead.
Jay Allison
Chairman and CEO, Comstock Resources
Perfect. Thank you, and good morning, everyone. I'd like to welcome all of you to the Comstock Resources Q1 2023 financial and operating results conference call. You can view a slide presentation during or after this call by going to our website at www.comstockresources.com and downloading the quarterly results presentation. There you'll find a presentation entitled First Quarter 2023 Results. I am Jay Allison, Chief Executive Officer of Comstock. With me is Roland Burns, our President and Chief Financial Officer, Dan Harrison, our Chief Operating Officer, and Ron Mills, our VP of Finance and Investor Relations. If you'll flip over to slide two. Please refer to slide two in our presentation to note that our discussions today will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of securities laws.
While we believe the expectations of such statements to be reasonable, there can be no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct. If you'll flip over to slide three, I wanna kind of address the issues. You know, I've read, I think all of the analyst reports that have been published and understand the concerns. You know, none are new concerns. We understand them. If you look at where oil is today, plus yesterday, it's down $7. If you look at where natural gas is yesterday and today it's down $0.20. You know, we all know that we're experiencing pressure with low natural gas prices currently in the short term. However, we're extremely positive on the outlook for natural gas in the future. Looking ahead several years, we recognize the growing need for natural gas around the world.
Our long-term goal is to be a significant supplier to the growing LNG market that is developing several hundred miles from our Haynesville Shale operations, including our emerging Western Haynesville area. Around the world today, over $1 trillion of natural gas infrastructure is being built. Over the next five years in the United States, we see more than $100 billion worth of new LNG plants being operational. We're currently in discussions to enter into long-term contracts with major LNG shippers who are following our new play with significant interest. To accomplish that goal, we must be great stewards of managing our dollars in this low gas price environment, while at the same time continuing to delineate our Western Haynesville asset. To that effect, we're continuing to run a two rig program that should result in 14 drilled wells by year-end 2023.
We also plan to wrap up our leasing efforts that we started almost three years ago. In Q1, we made great strides by materially adding to our acreage position, as you've noted. The well results in our traditional Haynesville area, where we had six to seven rigs running, continue to be very solid. Now we'll be down to five rigs in the next couple of weeks. Q1 still has some inflation baked into the well cost, but we see that abating in the next several quarters. We're continuing to reevaluate our rig count in our traditional Haynesville area, as well as our completion timing to be responsive to the weak price environment we're in, as we're very focused on maintaining the strong balance sheet that we've worked so hard to create last year.
In summary, we are implementing a practical business plan focused on the longer term cycle to position Comstock to benefit from the future growth in the LNG market. We'll monitor our plan to delineate our Western Haynesville play. We'll adjust it based upon the results that we achieve. We'll continue to prioritize our longer term goals while being very proactive to protect our strong balance sheet, which is allowing us to weather the current short term headwinds we see. If you go to slide three, we'll include some of the Q1 highlights. Our production increased 11% to 1.4 Bcf/d of gas equivalent. We had oil and gas sales of $390 million and operating cash flow of $255 million or $0.92 per diluted share.
Adjusted EBITDAX for the quarter was $293 million. Our adjusted net income for Q1 was $92 million or $0.33 per share. The financial results in the quarter reflect the weaker natural gas prices following the warm winter, the weather that we had. In Q1, we drilled 18 or 13.7 net operated Haynesville and Bossier horizontal wells, which had an average lateral length of 12,075 feet. Since our last update, we've connected 15 or 9.8 net operated wells to sales with an average initial production rate of 23 million cubic feet per day. These wells include 6 wells with lower IP rates in the liquid rich area of Panola County, which has associated liquid production.
We also announced our third successful exploratory well in our Western Haynesville play, the Gamble well, which had an initial production rate of 36 million cubic feet per day, which is a rate that we expect to produce it at. We had an active quarter acquiring additional acreage in our Western Haynesville play. Now I'll turn it over to Roland to discuss the financial results. Roland?
Roland Burns
President and CFO, Comstock Resources
Thanks, Jay. On slide four, we cover a quick summary of our financial results that we reported for Q1. As Jay said, our production in Q1 increased 11% to 1.4 BCF/d as compared to Q1 2022. Oil and gas sales in the quarter, including hedging gains, decreased by 4% to $390 million as lower natural gas prices offset the production growth that we had in the quarter. Our EBITDAX decreased by 12% to $293 million, and we generated $255 million of cash flow during the quarter, 14% less than 2022's Q1.
We reported adjusted net income of $92 million for Q1, and our earnings per share came in at $0.33 as compared to $0.51 in Q1 2022. On slide 5, we provide a breakdown of our natural gas price realizations in the quarter. During Q1, the quarterly NYMEX settlement price, which averaged $3.42, was substantially higher than the average Henry Hub spot price in the daily market of $2.67. During the quarter, we nominated 82% of our gas to be sold at the index prices tied to that contract settlement price, and we sold the other 18% of our gas in the daily spot market. The estimated NYMEX reference price for our sales in Q1 would've been $3.29.
Our realized gas price during Q1 averaged $2.98, reflecting a 31-cent differential to the reference price. That differential is higher than our normal for us due to the continued weaker Houston Ship Channel and Katy Hub prices that persisted during a good bit of Q1 due to the Freeport LNG facility shutdown. With the Freeport startup in late in the quarter, we've seen these price differentials along the Texas Gulf Coast tighten up somewhat. About 57% of our gas is tied to the Gulf Coast market indexes, and we are currently selling 21% of our gas directly to LNG shippers. In Q1, we were also 53% hedged, which improved our realized gas price to $3.07.
We've been using some of our excess transportation in the Haynesville to buy and resell third-party gas. This generated about $9 million of profit and improved our average gas price realization by another $0.07. On slide six, we detail our operating costs per Mcfe and our EBITDAX margin. Our operating cost per Mcfe averaged $0.83 in Q1, $0.07 higher than our Q4 rate.
